background.definition: The HSV genital infection is a lifelong sexually transmitted infection that may be asymptomatic, or may be intermittently and recurrently symptomatic.

list.listitem: Fifty million people in the United States have genital HSV infection.
The strongest predictor of HSV infection is lifetime number of sex partners.

Large studies indicate a seroprevalence rate of 21.9% in the adult population of the United States. The majority of these individuals, however, did not report a history of genital herpes. Thus, most infections are undiagnosed or subclinical.
HSV type I (HSV-1) and HSV type 2 (HSV-2) both can be associated with genital herpes infection. HSV-2 causes the majority of recurrent symptomatic infections in the genital tract.
HSV is spread via direct contact with infected mucous membranes or secretions. The incubation period is approximately 5 days from sexual contact.
Symptomatic infection begins with erythematous papules that progress to form vesicles. Vesicles will usually crust and heal within 1 to 3 weeks without the formation of scars.
Once infection has been established within the epithelia, the virus ascends along the sensory nerve roots to the dorsal root ganglion, where it remains latent.

Recurrent symptoms and shedding occur with reactivation. Subclinical viral shedding has been documented in more than 80% of HSV-2 seropositive persons who report no lesions. In a prospective cohort study of 498 adults with HSV-2 infections, viral shedding occurred during 10 percent of total observation days in patients without genital lesions.

list.listitem: Although many patients may request screening for genital HSV disease during a routine visit, screening of asymptomatic adolescents and adults with serological tests for HSV antibody provides no benefit in terms of health outcomes or transmission of disease. The USPSTF recommends against serologic screening for genital HSV. However, limited evidence suggests that screening for HSV does not lead to long-term psychosocial harms. B
Consistent use of condoms is associated with lower rates of infection with HSV-2 and should be recommended. B
Suppressive therapy with daily valacyclovir or famciclovir can reduce outbreaks by 70% to 80%. A
Daily treatment with valacyclovir 500 mg once a day has been shown to decrease the transmission of the disease in discordant heterosexual couples. B
Male circumcision in young adults reduces the risk of subsequent HSV infection (NNT = 40 over 24 months). B
Three phase 3 vaccine trials using HSV-2 glycoproteins were unsuccessful at meeting their primary endpoints; other vaccine candidates against genital herpes are in development. B

Glycoprotein-based HSV serologic testing may provide guidance for patients with recurrent genital symptoms and negative HSV PCR. C
PCR testing of CSF is the test of choice for suspected cases of HSV infection of the central nervous system. C

Rare in United States; may or may not be associated with quickly healing ulcer
Rare in United States; painless progressive ulcerations without lymphadenopathy

list.listitem: HSV-1 and HSV-2 are antigenically distinct viruses that share many common clinical characteristics.
HSV-1 is generally associated with oral lesions and HSV-2 is the more common in genital infections. Both viruses can, however, cause infection anywhere on the skin.

Symptomatic genital infection usually begins with a prodrome of nonspecific pain, burning, or tingling. This stage may include constitutional symptoms of fever, headache, malaise, and/or lymphadenopathy.

Classic symptomatic infection is then followed by the formation of clusters of uniform vesicles on an erythematous base. The vesicles typically progress to crusting and ulceration followed by complete healing without a scar. Vesicles and ulcers can form on the genitalia, perianal area, thighs, and buttocks.

In the United States, most young sexually active patients who present with genital vesicles or ulcers will have infection with HSV, syphilis, or chancroid. HSV is the most common cause of genital ulcer disease in the United States.

Viral cell culture used to be the diagnostic test of choice for the diagnosis of symptomatic genital herpes, but polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and serologic testing are also options. Sensitivity of viral culture rapidly diminishes as the lesions associated with HSV infection progress and/or heal. PCR is highly accurate in active ulcer disease and is now the test of choice. Patients who present with active genital ulcerations should also undergo serologic testing for syphilis.

HSV antibodies form in the weeks following infection and remain present for a lifetime. HSV-1 and HSV-2 antibodies differ in the area of glycoprotein G. Serologic testing for type-specific glycoprotein-G1 and glycoprotein-G2 HSV antibodies can, therefore, reliably distinguish between HSV-1 and HSV-2 infection. Because HSV-2 infection is generally sexually transmitted, the presence of HSV-2 antibodies correlates with anogenital infection. Patients with positive type-specific HSV-2 antibody testing should receive appropriate counseling about anogenital infection. HSV-1 antibodies do not distinguish infection in the oral or anogenital area.
Cytologic diagnosis via Pap test or Tzanck preparation is insensitive and nonspecific. These tests should not be used in the evaluation of ulcer disease.
Consider HSV in adults presenting with a first episode or recurrent painful genital vesicles, erosions or ulcers with or without associated prodrome of fever.
History and physical may not be highly accurate in diagnosing HSV but remain useful esp in resource-limited settings.
Patients with genital ulcers should be evaluated with serologic tests for syphilis and diagnostic tests for herpes infection.
The decision to give chronic suppressive therapy depends on a variety of factors, including the frequency and severity of outbreaks, the partner's HSV status, and whether condoms are used.
See for diagnostic strategy.
Oral acyclovir, valacyclovir or famciclovir, but not topical antivirals, appears to hasten symptom resolution of first genital herpes infection in men and women. B
Episodic therapy should be offered to patients who have infrequent recurrences. B
Suppressive therapy with oral acyclovir, valacyclovir or famciclovir appears to decrease outbreaks in patients with frequent recurrences (ie, ≥4 per year). It can reduce recurrences by 70% to 80%. B
Oral acyclovir, but not topical antivirals, appears to hasten symptom resolution of first genital herpes outbreak in men and women, based on low quality evidence from a Cochrane review.

For a first clinical episode of genital herpes, treatment options include acyclovir 400 mg orally 3 times a day for 7 to 10 days, acyclovir 200 mg orally 5 times a day for 7 to 10 days, famciclovir 250 mg orally 3 times a day for 7 to 10 days, or valacyclovir 1 g orally 3 times a day for 7 to 10 days.
Patients with severe disease, complications (eg, involvement of the eye or encephalitis) may require treatment with intravenous antivirals and hospitalization.

Suppressive therapy is recommended for patients with frequent recurrences of genital herpes (typically defined as ≥4 recurrences per year). Treatment options include acyclovir 400 mg twice a day, famciclovir 250 mg twice a day, valacyclovir 500 mg orally once a day, or valacyclovir 1 g orally once a day.

Episodic therapy should be offered to patients who have infrequent recurrences. Options for treatment of outbreaks include acyclovir 400 mg orally 3 times a day for 5 days, acyclovir 800 mg orally twice a day for 5 days, acyclovir 800 mg orally 3 times a day for 2 days, famciclovir 125 mg twice daily for 5 days, famciclovir 1000 mg orally twice daily for 1 day, valacyclovir 500 mg orally twice a day for 3 days, or valacyclovir 1 g once a day for 5 days.
In patients with cancer, acyclovir and valacyclovir are effective for prevention and treatment of herpes infection.
Use of echinacea purpurea did not affect the frequency of recurrence in a randomized crossover trial of 50 patients.

Patients diagnosed with genital herpes should be educated about the natural history of the disease, with emphasis on the potential for recurrent episodes, asymptomatic viral shedding, and the risks of sexual transmission.
During HSV outbreaks, patients should keep the affected area clean and dry to prevent secondary infection.
Suppressive treatment has been shown to decrease the rate of transmission of HSV-2 infection in discordant heterosexual couples.

Use of suppressive treatment, along with consistent condom use and avoidance of sexual activity during recurrences, should be discussed with patients interested in decreasing the likelihood of transmission.
The frequency of outbreaks often decreases with time. Interruption of suppressive therapy for HSV infection should be considered at regular intervals (ie, once or twice a year).
Hospitalize patients with severe disease or complications, such as disseminated infection, pneumonitis, hepatitis, or central nervous system complications.
Intravenous acyclovir therapy is recommended for patients with severe disease or complications. The regimen is acyclovir 5 to 10 mg per kg every 8 hours for 2 to 7 days or until clinical improvement.
Patients should then continue oral therapy until 10 days of total therapy is completed.
Approximately 90% of patients with a first episode HSV-2 genital infection will experience at least one recurrence within the first year. The median number of recurrences is 4 per year. B
Suppressive therapy with oral acyclovir, valacyclovir or famciclovir appears to decrease outbreaks in patients with frequent recurrences (ie, ≥4 per year). It can reduce recurrences by 70% to 80%. B

Primary lesions are defined as a first episode of genital symptoms in a patient with no history of any HSV disease. These primary lesions are frequently associated with systemic symptoms and can last 2 to 6 weeks. Recurrent outbreaks are usually milder.
Up to 50% of first-episode genital herpes are caused by HSV-1, but recurrences and subclinical shedding are much less frequent for HSV-1 genital infection than for HSV-2 genital infection.
Recurrence rates for HSV-2 vary, but 90% of patients will have at least one recurrence during the first year. The median number of recurrences for genital HSV-2 infection is 4 per year.
The majority of patients with symptomatic, first-episode genital HSV-2 infections experience recurrent episodes. Suppressive therapy reduces the frequency of genital recurrence by 70% to 80%.
Cesarean delivery should be performed on women with primary or recurrent HSV infection who have active genital lesions or prodromal symptoms at the time of delivery.
In women with no active lesions or prodromal symptoms during labor, cesarean delivery should not be performed on the basis of a history of recurrent disease.
Asymptomatic pregnant women should not be routinely screened for HSV virus during pregnancy to prevent neonatal HSV infection.
Although antiviral prophylaxis during the third trimester reduces the risk of outbreaks and cesarean delivery, its safety to the neonate is not well established.

Based on a Cochrane review, there is insufficient evidence for the efficacy of systemic antivirals for neonatal HSV infection, including more bioavailable agents like valacyclovir and valganciclovir. However, they remain first-line treatment considering the seriousness of neonatal HSV and the difficulty in conducting adequately powered trials for this rare neonatal infection.
